questions.question: Describe how a group should evaluate design sketches against a brief and give an example of a well-reasoned judgement.
questions.expected_answer: Place the shared specifications down the side of a table and the sketches across the top; for each cell decide whether the design as drawn is likely to meet the specification, mark a tick, cross or question mark, and write a short reason in the language of the term that points to an investigation, lesson or specification. Then list at least two advantages and two disadvantages under each idea and advise each learner which idea is the stronger starting point, leaving the decision to the owner. Example: rigidity, cross, because the upper panels have single straw diagonals that will buckle in compression and there is no internal bracing, so the section is likely to twist under a sideways push.

questions.question: Give four rules for giving constructive criticism and three for receiving it.
questions.expected_answer: Giving: criticise the design, not the designer; start with what works; be specific and tie every comment to the brief or an investigation; suggest rather than instruct, and give everyone equal time. Receiving: listen to the whole comment before responding and write it down; ask a question to understand rather than defending; thank the person and decide later, alone, what to change, recording a reason for any comment you reject.

questions.question: Explain how a learner should adapt and improve a design after group evaluation, and why the original sketch must be kept.
questions.expected_answer: Work through the comments one at a time and make a specific change for each with a reason tied to a specification or investigation, for example redrawing the base to 150 millimetres for the footprint, adding X bracing to the lower panels and internal string bracing for rigidity, or thickening the base plate and adding webs to carry a canopy's top weight. Draw the improved design as a third sketch or mark the changes clearly on the chosen one, write a paragraph on which idea was chosen, which comments were accepted or rejected and why, and what was borrowed, then re-check against every specification. The original is kept because the improvement, and therefore the design process, is only visible when before and after both exist.
